In this lab you will estimate the distribution of annual minimum temperatures at Houston Hobby Airport and quantify how uncertain those estimates are.
The question running through the lab is: how rare is a winter as cold as 2021, and how confident are you in that answer?

## Background

Houston Hobby Airport (GHCN station USW00012918) has daily minimum temperature records from 1930 to the present.
The file `houston-hobby-annual-tmin.csv` contains the coldest temperature recorded in each year, in degrees Celsius.

A Normal distribution is not the theoretically best choice for annual minimum temperatures (extreme value theory in week 4 gives a better one), but it is a decent approximation and a useful example for practicing estimation methods.

You will fit a Normal to the data by MLE, estimate the same parameters with a Bayesian conjugate prior, and bootstrap the return period.
The payoff is the side-by-side comparison: how do the three approaches agree, and where do they disagree?

## Analysis

### Fitting a Normal by MLE

```{julia}
#| solution: false
y = annmin.tmin_c
n = length(y)
μ_hat = mean(y)
σ_hat = std(y)
@printf("MLE: μ̂ = %.2f °C, σ̂ = %.2f °C, n = %d", μ_hat, σ_hat, n)
```

For the Normal, the MLE and the method of moments give the same answer: the sample mean and the sample standard deviation.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
fig = Figure(; size=(700, 300))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel=L"\text{annual minimum temperature (°C)}", ylabel="density")
hist!(ax, y; bins=15, normalization=:pdf, color=(colors[1], 0.5))
xs = range(minimum(y) - 3, maximum(y) + 3; length=300)
lines!(ax, xs, pdf.(Normal(μ_hat, σ_hat), xs); linewidth=3, color=colors[2], label="fitted Normal")
axislegend(ax; position=:lt)
fig
```

### Return period of the 2021 freeze

From week 1, the return period of a level $x_0$ is $T = 1/p$.
For cold extremes, $p = P(X \le x_0)$: the probability of falling *below* the threshold in a given year.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
x_2021 = -9.3
fit_mle = Normal(μ_hat, σ_hat)
p_mle = cdf(fit_mle, x_2021)
T_mle = 1 / p_mle
@printf("MLE return period of %.1f °C: %.1f years", x_2021, T_mle)
```

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| output: false
y_sorted = sort(y)
p_obs = (1:n) ./ (n + 1)
T_obs = 1 ./ p_obs
Ts = 10 .^ range(0.01, 2.5; length=300)
B = 5000
```

### Bayesian estimation

A conjugate prior for the Normal with known variance is another Normal distribution on $\mu$.
Use a prior $\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(-3, 5^2)$ (wide enough to be weakly informative) and treat $\sigma$ as known at $\hat\sigma$.

The posterior is $\mu \mid y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_{\text{post}}, \sigma_{\text{post}}^2)$ where:

$$
\sigma_{\text{post}}^2 = \left(\frac{n}{\hat\sigma^2} + \frac{1}{\sigma_{\text{prior}}^2}\right)^{-1}, \qquad \mu_{\text{post}} = \sigma_{\text{post}}^2 \left(\frac{n \bar y}{\hat\sigma^2} + \frac{\mu_{\text{prior}}}{\sigma_{\text{prior}}^2}\right)
$$

```{julia}
μ_prior = -3
σ_prior = 5

σ2_post = 1 / (n / σ_hat^2 + 1 / σ_prior^2)
μ_post = σ2_post * (n * μ_hat / σ_hat^2 + μ_prior / σ_prior^2)

@printf("Posterior: μ_post = %.2f °C, σ_post = %.2f °C", μ_post, sqrt(σ2_post))
```

### Bootstrap

Resample the $n$ annual minima with replacement, refit the Normal each time, and recompute the return period of the 2021 freeze.

```{julia}
μ_boot = Vector{Float64}(undef, B)
σ_boot = Vector{Float64}(undef, B)
T_boot = Vector{Float64}(undef, B)
for b in 1:B
    y_b = sample(rng, y, n; replace=true)
    μ_boot[b] = mean(y_b)
    σ_boot[b] = std(y_b)
    p_b = cdf(Normal(μ_boot[b], σ_boot[b]), x_2021)
    T_boot[b] = 1 / p_b
end
@printf("Bootstrap median return period: %.1f years", median(T_boot))
```

### Bayesian return period uncertainty

Draw 5,000 samples of $\mu$ from the posterior and compute the return period for each.

```{julia}
μ_draws = rand(rng, Normal(μ_post, sqrt(σ2_post)), B)

T_bayes = Vector{Float64}(undef, B)
for b in 1:B
    p_b = cdf(Normal(μ_draws[b], σ_hat), x_2021)
    T_bayes[b] = 1 / p_b
end
@printf("Bayesian median return period: %.1f years", median(T_bayes))
```

### Return period plots with uncertainty

Each gray line is one draw; the solid line is the MLE best fit.

```{julia}
n_show = 200
mle_curve = quantile.(Normal(μ_hat, σ_hat), 1 ./ Ts)

fig = Figure(; size=(900, 350))

ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale=log10, xlabel="return period (years)",
    ylabel="annual minimum temperature (°C)", title="Bootstrap")
lines!(ax1, Ts, quantile.(Normal(μ_boot[1], σ_boot[1]), 1 ./ Ts); color=(:gray, 0.15), label="bootstrap draws")
for b in 2:n_show
    lines!(ax1, Ts, quantile.(Normal(μ_boot[b], σ_boot[b]), 1 ./ Ts); color=(:gray, 0.15))
end
lines!(ax1, Ts, mle_curve; color=colors[2], linewidth=2, label="MLE fit")
scatter!(ax1, T_obs, y_sorted; color=colors[1], markersize=6, label="observed years")
axislegend(ax1; position=:rt)

ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2]; xscale=log10, xlabel="return period (years)",
    ylabel="annual minimum temperature (°C)", title="Bayesian")
lines!(ax2, Ts, quantile.(Normal(μ_draws[1], σ_hat), 1 ./ Ts); color=(:gray, 0.15), label="Bayesian draws")
for b in 2:n_show
    lines!(ax2, Ts, quantile.(Normal(μ_draws[b], σ_hat), 1 ./ Ts); color=(:gray, 0.15))
end
lines!(ax2, Ts, mle_curve; color=colors[2], linewidth=2, label="MLE fit")
scatter!(ax2, T_obs, y_sorted; color=colors[1], markersize=6, label="observed years")
axislegend(ax2; position=:rt)

fig
```

### Autocorrelation

```{julia}
#| solution: false
fig = Figure(; size=(700, 250))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel="lag (years)", ylabel="autocorrelation")
acf_vals = autocor(y, 1:15)
barplot!(ax, 1:15, acf_vals; color=colors[1])
hlines!(ax, 1.96 / sqrt(n) .* [-1, 1]; color=:gray50, linestyle=:dash, label="white noise band")
axislegend(ax; position=:rt)
fig
```

The dashed lines show the range you would expect from white noise (independent draws): $\pm 1.96/\sqrt{n}$.
The autocorrelations all fall inside this band, so year-to-year persistence is not a concern for this series.
If they were large, the plain bootstrap would underestimate uncertainty because resampling individual years destroys the dependence structure.

## Exercises

### How does the posterior compare to the MLE?

**Your answer:** How does the posterior mean compare to the MLE?
Why are they so similar here, and when would you expect them to differ?

::: {.answer}

```{julia}
#| echo: false
# Your code here
```

The posterior mean (−4.33 °C) is almost the same as the MLE (−4.34 °C).
This makes sense because the prior has a large standard deviation (5), so it is not very confident and carries little weight.
With 88 years of data, the data carries far more weight than the prior, so the posterior ends up close to the MLE.
They would differ more if the prior were stronger (a smaller σ_prior) or if we had a shorter record, since then the data would not dominate as much.

:::

### Compare the 50-year return level

**Your answer:** Compute the 50-year return level (the temperature exceeded once in 50 years on the cold side) from the MLE fit, and give bootstrap and Bayesian 95% intervals for it.

::: {.answer}

```{julia}
p50 = 1 / 50
level_mle = quantile(Normal(μ_hat, σ_hat), p50)

level_boot = quantile.(Normal.(μ_boot, σ_boot), p50)
ci_boot = quantile(level_boot, [0.025, 0.975])

level_bayes = quantile.(Normal.(μ_draws, σ_hat), p50)
ci_bayes = quantile(level_bayes, [0.025, 0.975])

@printf("MLE 50-year return level: %.2f °C", level_mle)
@printf("Bootstrap 95%% interval: [%.2f, %.2f] °C", ci_boot[1], ci_boot[2])
@printf("Bayesian 95%% interval: [%.2f, %.2f] °C", ci_bayes[1], ci_bayes[2])
```

The MLE gives one best guess for the 50-year return level, but the bootstrap and Bayesian intervals show how much that guess could change given only 88 years of data.

:::

### Does the Normal fit the tail?

**Your answer:** Look at the return period plots from the analysis section, especially for return periods above 50 years.
The observed coldest events fall below the fitted curve.
What does this tell you about the Normal as a model for extreme cold in Houston?
Why might the coldest winters be colder than a Normal predicts?

::: {.answer}

In the return period plots, the coldest years (the blue dots) fall below both fitted curves once the return period is past about 20 to 30 years.
This means the Normal model predicts these cold events should be rarer than they really are. Its tails are too thin to capture how cold the coldest years actually get.

My guess is that ordinary winters and truly extreme ones like 2021 come from different processes.
Normal year-to-year variation is likely just typical weather noise, but the most extreme cold snaps are probably caused by rare Arctic air outbreaks reaching into Texas. That is a different mechanism.
Fitting one Normal to the whole record assumes it is all one process, when the data might actually contain two.
This is the kind of situation extreme value theory (week 4) is designed for, since it uses distributions with heavier tails that do not underestimate the worst case.

:::

### Why is the bootstrap band wider than the Bayesian band?

**Your answer:** Look at the return period plots again.
The bootstrap draws spread wider than the Bayesian draws, especially in the tail.
Why?
Hint: think about what each method holds fixed and what it varies.

::: {.answer}

The two methods do not account for the same sources of uncertainty.
In our Bayesian setup, only $\mu$ varies. We drew 5,000 samples of $\mu$ from the posterior and kept $\sigma$ fixed at $\hat\sigma$ the whole time.
The bootstrap refits both $\mu$ and $\sigma$ on every one of its 5,000 resamples.

This matters because if a resample happens to include more cold years by chance, it does not just shift the mean. It also raises $\hat\sigma$, which stretches the tail of the fitted distribution further out.
The bootstrap picks up that extra variability, but our Bayesian approach cannot, since we held $\sigma$ fixed by assumption.
So the Bayesian interval ends up narrower than it probably should, simply because of how we set up the model (a prior only on $\mu$, not $\sigma$).
If we had also put a prior on $\sigma$ and let it vary, I would expect the Bayesian band to widen and look more like the bootstrap's.

:::

### Wrapping up

**Your answer:** A city planner asks you: how rare is a winter as cold as 2021?
Give a point estimate and a plausible range, and explain in one or two sentences why the range matters more than the point estimate.

::: {.answer}

```{julia}
ci_T_boot = quantile(T_boot, [0.025, 0.975])
ci_T_bayes = quantile(T_bayes, [0.025, 0.975])

@printf("MLE return period: %.1f years", T_mle)
@printf("Bootstrap 95%% interval: [%.1f, %.1f] years", ci_T_boot[1], ci_T_boot[2])
@printf("Bayesian 95%% interval: [%.1f, %.1f] years", ci_T_bayes[1], ci_T_bayes[2])
```

The MLE says the 2021 freeze is roughly a 1-in-15-year event, but the 95% interval is wide: 8 to 36 years from the bootstrap, and 10 to 22 years from the Bayesian approach.
The planner cannot tell the difference between "a fairly common cold snap" and "a rare multi-decade event" from this record and this model, and those two answers would lead to very different decisions about infrastructure spending.

:::
